question: Does this survey give a mathematically sound, reproducible, and empirically representative account of intrinsic-dimension estimation, and how far do its estimator rankings and practical recommendations generalize beyond its selected classical methods, synthetic manifolds, scales, and tuning protocol?

key_findings.claim: The paper's strongest conceptual warning is that a finite point cloud has no identifiable intrinsic dimension without assumptions about the support or generative model from which it was sampled.
key_findings.evidence: Any finite set can be embedded in a zero-dimensional manifold and can also be interpolated by a curve, so the sample alone does not determine a unique manifold dimension. The survey accordingly frames estimation through distributional, geometric, regularity, reach, and scale assumptions. This is a more honest foundation than treating intrinsic dimension as an observable property of an arbitrary matrix.

anchors.section: Section 1, non-identifiability of dimension from finite samples

key_findings.claim: Its most useful synthesis is a taxonomy by the geometric information consumed by an estimator: tangent directions, parametric distance or angle distributions, and topological or metric scaling invariants.
key_findings.evidence: The survey derives or summarizes lPCA, kernel PCA, MDS and direction-based estimators; volume-growth, correlation, packing, likelihood, ratio, angle and concentration estimators; and PH0/MST, k-nearest-neighbor graph and magnitude estimators. It then separately discusses local, global and bilocal use. This organization exposes shared mechanisms and scale requirements more clearly than a single local-versus-global split, although several estimators cross categories.

anchors.section: Sections 2.4-2.5, other approaches and local/global behavior

key_findings.claim: Within the tested cohort there is no universal winner: ESS is the strongest broad default reported outside the nonlinear subset, while most tested estimators fail to estimate nonlinear dimensions above roughly six satisfactorily.
key_findings.evidence: The authors compare about twenty implementations over approximately twenty-five synthetic benchmark manifolds, four sample sizes from 625 to 5,000, multiple hyperparameter grids, and generally twenty random samples per configuration. They report substantial method-by-manifold and method-by-scale variation, widespread high-dimensional underestimation, especially poor performance on nonlinear high-dimensional data, and comparatively strong ESS performance. These are conditional empirical findings, not field-wide rankings, because modern learned estimators and several curvature-adaptive methods are outside the main cohort.

anchors.section: Section 3.3, aggregate accuracy and sample-efficiency results

key_findings.claim: The hyperparameter comparison is optimistic because its headline oracle and fixed settings are selected and scored on the same benchmark samples or manifold collection.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix C defines a per-estimator, per-manifold best setting using known true dimension and reports the selected result on the same twenty samples. The fixed absolute and relative settings are likewise chosen across the benchmark rather than on held-out manifolds. There is no nested selection, independent test collection, or correction for the differing number of candidate settings. Moreover, selection minimizes absolute bias of an averaged estimate rather than average pointwise absolute error, so positive and negative errors can cancel and high-variance candidates can win.

key_findings.claim: The benchmark is broad within standard synthetic-manifold practice but narrow in topology, dimension structure, sampling assumptions, and real-world validity.
key_findings.evidence: Most benchmark families are smooth, constant-dimensional, i.i.d. samples with known Euclidean metric and are diffeomorphic to spheres or cubes; SO(n) supplies only limited topological variety. The evaluation lacks stratified or singular spaces, mixed or point-varying dimension, learned or task-conditioned metrics, non-i.i.d. streams, categorical data, and real datasets with independently defensible ground truth. The Gaussian case is also noncompact and has full ambient support, making its declared intrinsic dimension depend on a metric-measure rather than literal support interpretation.

Section 4, acknowledged need for richer manifolds and real-data work

key_findings.claim: The main experiment does not test the recent learned density, likelihood, score, or diffusion estimators that are most relevant to high-dimensional local dimension estimation.
key_findings.evidence: LIDL and diffusion-based approaches are mentioned briefly among other estimators, but the main comparison remains dominated by classical neighborhood, angle, spectral and scaling techniques. FLIPD, LIDL, diffusion-score normal-bundle methods, curvature-adapted PCA and automatic neighborhood-selection methods are absent. The conclusions that ESS or parametric methods are best and that nonlinear dimension above six is unsatisfactory therefore describe the selected cohort rather than the state of all available methods.

key_findings.claim: The stated capacity-dimension formula has the wrong sign, and the accompanying claim that capacity and topological dimensions coincide whenever both exist is false.
key_findings.evidence: The paper writes capacity dimension as lim log N(r)/log r as r tends to zero. Since a d-dimensional covering number scales as N(r) approximately r^{-d}, that expression gives -d; the denominator should be log(1/r), or an explicit minus sign is needed. It then says capacity dimension equals topological dimension whenever both exist, contradicted by standard fractals such as the Cantor set, whose topological dimension is zero and box/capacity dimension is log 2 divided by log 3. The scale-dependent estimator inherits the sign error.

key_findings.claim: Three foundational estimator formulas contain visible indexing or sign errors: the lPCA eigengap inequality, its variance sum, and the TwoNN CDF relation.
key_findings.evidence: For lPCA, the prose seeks a large eigenvalue ratio but the displayed minimum uses lambda_u/lambda_{u+1} less than beta for beta greater than one; the stated rule requires the opposite inequality. Its cumulative-variance formula sums through N even though the covariance spectrum was introduced with D eigenvalues. For TwoNN, rho=r_2/r_1 is at least one and has Pareto survival rho^{-d}, so log(1-F(rho))/log rho equals -d, not d as printed. These errors are likely repairable typographical defects, but they make direct implementation from the survey unsafe.

anchors.section: Section 2.1.1, lPCA eigengap and cumulative-variance equations

key_findings.claim: The claimed ball-to-sphere Wasserstein-2 distance is unnormalized and its asserted exponential convergence with dimension is wrong.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed radial shell integral omits normalization by the unit-ball volume, so it is not the Wasserstein distance between probability measures. For the normalized uniform d-ball, the radius density is d r^{d-1}; coupling radial points to the sphere gives W_2 squared equal to E[(1-R)^2]=2/((d+1)(d+2)). Thus W_2 is asymptotically sqrt(2)/d, a polynomial rather than exponential rate. The qualitative boundary-concentration intuition survives, but not the formula or rate claim used to explain underestimation.

key_findings.claim: Appendix C's formal definition of the oracle 'best estimate' returns an error magnitude, not the dimension estimate shown in the tables.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines d-hat_best(E,M) as the minimum over hyperparameters of |d-hat(E,M,H)-d(M)|. That scalar is the minimum absolute error. The surrounding text and table columns instead report the estimate produced by a selected hyperparameter. A correct definition must first take an argmin and then evaluate d-hat at the selected setting, with a tie rule. This mismatch also obscures whether selection is based on a mean estimate or individual runs.

anchors.section: Appendix C, definition of the best-hyperparameter estimate

key_findings.claim: Very low reported variance can be an artifact of discrete local estimates, median aggregation, or rounding and is not by itself evidence of reliable dimension recovery.
key_findings.evidence: Several lPCA configurations output integer local dimensions and aggregate them by a median, producing zero or near-zero sample variance even when the common integer is biased. The paper notices this aggregation effect, but the large result tables can visually reward stability independently of correctness. Accuracy, dispersion, calibration across scales, and the frequency of throttling should be reported together.

anchors.section: Section 3.3, variability and aggregate benchmark results
Appendix C, per-manifold means and standard deviations

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies a valuable 'throttling' mechanism: neighborhood size can impose a hard or rapidly growing ceiling on recoverable dimension.
key_findings.evidence: Tangential estimators cannot return a rank above that supported by their local sample, giving at least linear throttling, while bounded-valence graph or probabilistic occupancy mechanisms can require neighborhood size to grow exponentially or quadratically with dimension. This reframes apparently intrinsic high-dimensional failure as an interaction among estimator, scale, sample size and dimension. The proposed diagnostic—compare the estimate with the neighborhood-imposed ceiling and warn users—translates directly into safer software.

anchors.section: Section 4, throttling as a practical recommendation

key_findings.claim: The noise and outlier conclusions are useful stress tests but too narrow and inconsistently reported to support general robustness claims.
key_findings.evidence: Gaussian noise is tested on only S6, S10 and SO(4), with parameters chosen on clean S10, and the outlier generator multiplies coordinates of selected existing points by random factors rather than sampling diverse contamination processes. The text says final noise results are medians over twenty runs, one Figure 10 caption says averages over ten, and Appendix E labels entries as means with standard deviations. There are no anisotropic, heteroscedastic, tangent-aligned, missing-data or adversarial noise models, and the observed outlier tolerance is specific to Algorithm 1.

key_findings.claim: The curvature study supports a hypothesis about lPCA and MLE in its chosen settings, not the broad conclusion that parametric estimators are generally more curvature-robust than tangential ones.
key_findings.evidence: The study compares only lPCA with one threshold rule against MLE over paraboloids sampled near the origin and a torus, using fixed neighborhood grids and unequal repetition counts. It observes stronger curvature-related bias for lPCA and modest MLE underestimation, but it does not include other members of either family, curvature-adapted PCA, automatic scale selection, matched compute, or varied densities. Family-level causal language exceeds this two-method experiment.

key_findings.claim: Despite calling its literature search systematic, the paper does not provide the protocol needed for a reproducible systematic review.
key_findings.evidence: The method reports Google Scholar searches for two broad phrases and an emphasis on work since 2015, but gives no search dates, complete query strings, database coverage, language rules, inclusion or exclusion criteria, duplicate handling, screening counts, extraction form, quality appraisal, reviewer agreement, or released literature corpus. The authors explicitly say the survey is not comprehensive. It is therefore a substantial narrative and experimental survey, not a systematic review in the evidence-synthesis sense.

anchors.section: End of Section 1, search description, scope and non-comprehensiveness caveat

key_findings.claim: The linked code is a useful, tested estimator library, but the paper's exact numerical study is not fully reproducible from the currently linked branch.
key_findings.evidence: The paper links an augmented scikit-dimension fork and describes added implementations including GeoMLE, GRIDE, CDim, WODCap, CorrInt, packing, magnitude and PH0. A 2026-08-23 audit of the linked default branch at commit d7c6248a591b761373dbeb3abbcb32ed2c83c232 found library code, documentation, tests and CI, but not the paper's full benchmark, noise and curvature scripts, raw result tables, seeds, environment lock or an exact paper commit. The live branch also postdates submission. The algorithms are reusable; the reported experiment is not push-button reproducible from that branch alone.

method.core_idea: Unify intrinsic-dimension estimators by the local or global geometric signal they measure, implement a broader common estimator set, and stress-test accuracy as sample size, hyperparameters, noise and curvature vary.
method.mechanism: The survey derives estimator families from tangent spectra, covering and correlation growth, nearest-neighbor distance ratios, angle distributions, concentration statistics, persistent-homology or graph-length scaling, and metric magnitude. Its empirical study applies these implementations to known-dimensional synthetic manifolds at N=625, 1,250, 2,500 and 5,000, generally repeats each setting twenty times, compares oracle-selected and globally fixed hyperparameters, and runs targeted aggregation, scale, threshold, noise, outlier and curvature studies.
assumptions: Samples arise from, or concentrate near, a meaningful lower-dimensional geometric or metric-measure object.
The selected ambient metric and feature representation preserve the geometry relevant to the desired dimension estimand.
Local neighborhoods are sufficiently populated to approximate tangent, density, angle or scaling laws without crossing curvature, boundaries or density changes.
Most benchmark interpretations assume smooth, constant-dimensional manifolds sampled independently from prescribed distributions.
Known synthetic dimension is a suitable proxy for real-data ground truth and estimator rankings transfer beyond the benchmark family.
Hyperparameter grids and the aggregation rule provide a fair opportunity for each estimator despite unequal computational costs and scale requirements.

techniques.role: Groups estimators by tangential, parametric, and topological or metric information rather than only by local versus global output.
Estimates tangent rank from neighborhood covariance spectra and exposes threshold, aggregation, curvature and rank-throttling effects.
Uses nearest-neighbor radii, ratios, volumes, angles and likelihood laws for local or global dimension estimates.
Infers dimension as a slope in correlation, covering, persistent-homology, graph-length or magnitude scaling.
Sweeps neighborhood sizes, thresholds and other method-specific settings to measure sensitivity and oracle performance.
Perturbs selected manifolds with Gaussian noise or multiplicative coordinate outliers to probe robustness.
Varies paraboloid and torus curvature to compare lPCA and MLE responses at multiple neighborhood sizes.
Relates estimator output ceilings to neighborhood cardinality and dimension-dependent sample requirements.

evaluations.setting: Approximately twenty-five known-dimensional synthetic manifold datasets spanning intrinsic dimensions 1-70, ambient dimensions 3-96, and sample sizes 625, 1,250, 2,500 and 5,000.
evaluations.metric: Mean or aggregated dimension estimate, absolute deviation from known dimension, dispersion over generally twenty samples, and qualitative success across dataset subsets.
evaluations.result: No estimator dominates; ESS is the strongest broad performer in the selected non-neural cohort outside the nonlinear subset, while most methods underestimate high dimension and fail on nonlinear manifolds above about dimension six.
evaluations.baseline: Roughly twenty classical tangential, likelihood, distance, angle, concentration, graph, persistent-homology and magnitude implementations under method-specific grids.

evaluations.setting: Per-manifold oracle, globally fixed absolute, and dimension-relative hyperparameter comparisons across Appendix C.
evaluations.metric: Distance between the averaged estimate and known dimension, plus reported standard deviation or robust aggregate statistics.
evaluations.result: Tuning strongly changes rankings and fixed settings transfer poorly across geometries; however, oracle and fixed settings are selected in sample, so their reported performance is optimistic.
evaluations.baseline: Each estimator's alternative hyperparameter settings over the same benchmark and samples.

evaluations.setting: Neighborhood-size sweeps for local estimators and dimension-dependent analysis of rank, graph and occupancy constraints.
evaluations.metric: Estimated dimension as a function of k, true dimension and the estimator's attainable ceiling.
evaluations.result: Small neighborhoods can linearly, quadratically or exponentially throttle estimates, explaining a substantial class of high-dimensional underestimation.
evaluations.baseline: Larger-neighborhood settings and theoretical sample-growth expectations.

evaluations.setting: lPCA threshold and aggregation study over multiple benchmark manifolds.
evaluations.metric: Bias and variability under eigengap, variance-retention, probabilistic and aggregation choices.
evaluations.result: lPCA can be competitive when tuned, but threshold and aggregation choices substantially alter results; discrete medians can create deceptively zero variance.
evaluations.baseline: Alternative lPCA thresholds and mean versus median aggregation.

evaluations.setting: PH0 versus k-nearest-neighbor graph scaling, with a separate finite-size magnitude analysis in Appendices A and B.
evaluations.metric: Slope-derived dimension error and variability as sample size or scale range changes.
evaluations.result: PH0 is broadly comparable to the related graph estimator with lower observed variance in several settings, while magnitude requires much larger effective scale and sample support.
evaluations.baseline: Matched graph-scaling variants and finite-sample magnitude curves.

evaluations.setting: Gaussian perturbations on S6, S10 and SO(4), plus multiplicative-coordinate outliers from Algorithm 1.
evaluations.metric: Reported mean or median estimated dimension and dispersion as noise or outlier fraction increases.
evaluations.result: Gaussian noise degrades most estimators; the selected outlier process is often tolerated except notably by FisherS, but inconsistent run and aggregation descriptions weaken exact comparison.
evaluations.baseline: The same estimators and hyperparameters on clean samples.

evaluations.setting: Paraboloid and torus curvature sweeps comparing lPCA and MLE over neighborhood sizes.
evaluations.metric: Dimension estimate as principal curvature and k vary.
evaluations.result: lPCA exhibits stronger curvature-associated bias in the chosen configuration, whereas MLE tends toward modest underestimation; two methods are insufficient to establish a family-wide robustness hierarchy.
evaluations.baseline: Low-curvature samples and alternative k values for the same two estimators.

evaluations.setting: Real, mixed-dimensional, singular, learned-representation, or task-relevant data with independently validated ground truth.
evaluations.metric: External validity, pointwise calibration, downstream utility and robustness to representation changes.
evaluations.baseline: Modern mixed-dimensional, score-based, topology-rich and task-conditioned benchmarks.

limitations: The literature search is not reproducible as a systematic review and explicitly is not comprehensive.
Several displayed formulas have consequential sign, normalization, indexing or argmin errors.
Oracle and globally fixed hyperparameters are selected and evaluated on the same samples or manifold collection without nested validation.
Unequal hyperparameter-grid sizes give estimators unequal chances to benefit from oracle selection.
The benchmark mostly contains smooth, constant-dimensional, simply structured synthetic manifolds with known Euclidean metric.
Modern learned likelihood, score, diffusion, curvature-adaptive and automatic-scale methods are omitted from the main empirical cohort.
There are no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, nested uncertainty estimates, or correction for repeated model selection.
Runtime and memory are not normalized; expensive methods are excluded based partly on the available implementations, making comparison implementation-dependent.
Sample-efficiency claims are restricted mainly to N between 625 and 5,000 and low intrinsic dimensions, so asymptotic scaling is untested.
Noise, outlier and curvature studies vary only a few generators and use inconsistent repetitions or summary-statistic descriptions.
The linked current code branch does not pin the exact paper revision, environment, seeds, raw results or all experiment scripts.
failure_modes: Neighborhood rank or occupancy ceilings throttle estimated dimension before the estimator reaches its nominal asymptotic regime.
Curvature, boundaries, nonuniform density and finite samples violate locally flat or homogeneous Poisson assumptions.
Small ambient noise can change literal support dimension to the ambient dimension even when the intended latent or effective dimension is unchanged.
Global estimates collapse mixtures of strata or point-varying dimensions into a misleading scalar.
Oracle tuning overfits benchmark idiosyncrasies and can reverse method rankings on unseen geometries or representations.
Median aggregation and integer local outputs can hide instability or bias behind zero empirical variance.
Covering, correlation and slope estimators can fit the wrong finite-scale region and mistake pre-asymptotic behavior for dimension.
Nearest-neighbor methods can become dominated by distance concentration or density variation in high ambient dimension.
Support dimension, effective metric-measure dimension, representation dimension and task-relevant dimension can disagree while each remains mathematically coherent.
A method that succeeds on spheres and cubes can fail under topology, embedding, feature-map or domain transformations that preserve true dimension.
reusable_insights: State the dimension estimand and generative assumptions before choosing an estimator; a finite cloud alone does not identify one.
Classify estimators by the geometric statistic they consume, then separately record locality, scale and aggregation behavior.
Treat neighborhood size as part of the estimator and emit a warning when k creates a rank or occupancy ceiling near the returned dimension.
Evaluate tuning with held-out manifold families or nested simulation, not an oracle selected on the reported samples.
Report error, dispersion, calibration over scales, computational cost and failure frequency together.
Use benchmark families with controlled topology, curvature, density, noise, codimension, singularity and representation shifts.
Distinguish literal support dimension from effective, local and task-relevant dimension under noise.
Preserve formula-level executable tests in a survey codebase so sign, normalization and indexing errors cannot enter reference equations.
Compare classical and learned estimators under matched information, compute and hyperparameter-selection budgets.
Archive the exact code commit, environment, seeds, generated datasets and raw tables used for every survey experiment.
open_questions: Can scale be selected from data without known dimension while retaining finite-sample guarantees under boundaries, curvature and density variation?
What benchmark split best tests transfer across unseen topology, embedding, codimension, representation and sampling process?
How should uncertainty over local dimension, scale and model assumptions be propagated into one interpretable output?
Can a unified estimator detect stratification or singularity and return pointwise dimensions instead of forcing a global scalar?
When should practitioners estimate support dimension, effective metric-measure dimension, latent generative dimension or task-relevant dimension?
Which learned score or likelihood estimators outperform well-tuned classical methods after matched compute, architecture selection and unknown-scale selection?
Can throttling diagnostics yield principled sample-size requirements or abstention rules before an expensive benchmark run?
How can real-data dimension claims be externally validated when ground truth is not observable?
Do rankings remain stable under dimension-preserving transformations across images, language, graphs and scientific representations?
What minimal reproducibility bundle would let a living survey add estimators and benchmarks without changing historical comparisons?

competitive_landscape.title: Scikit-dimension: a Python package for intrinsic dimension estimation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct software and benchmark predecessor providing a uniform API, synthetic generators, tests and a comparison over more than 500 real and synthetic datasets.
competitive_landscape.difference: The reviewed paper builds on an augmented fork and adds several estimators plus deeper known-ground-truth hyperparameter, noise and curvature studies, but it is not the first unified package or broad benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: LIDL: Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation Using Approximate Likelihood
competitive_landscape.relationship: Learned likelihood competitor for local intrinsic dimension in very high ambient dimension.
competitive_landscape.difference: LIDL reports scaling to thousands of dimensions and lies outside the main benchmark; it broadens the method space but introduces density-model, ambient-extension, architecture and noise-scale dependence.

competitive_landscape.title: CA-PCA: Manifold Dimension Estimation, Adapted for Curvature
competitive_landscape.relationship: Pre-submission curvature-adapted PCA method directly relevant to the survey's tangential-estimator curvature study.
competitive_landscape.difference: CA-PCA calibrates spectra against a quadratic rather than flat local model; its omission means the lPCA-versus-MLE experiment does not cover the main curvature-specific tangential alternative.

competitive_landscape.title: Diffusion Models Encode the Intrinsic Dimension of Data Manifolds
competitive_landscape.relationship: Score-based theoretical and empirical competitor that extracts normal-bundle dimension information from diffusion models.
competitive_landscape.difference: It targets image-scale learned distributions and a different information regime than nearest-neighbor estimators, but its training, representation and diffusion-time choices are additional sources of uncertainty absent from the classical benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: A Geometric View of Data Complexity: Efficient Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation with Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: FLIPD is a direct modern local-dimension competitor based on a Fokker-Planck identity and one pretrained diffusion model.
competitive_landscape.difference: It supports mixed-dimensional synthetic and large image settings omitted by the survey and can operate at Stable Diffusion scale, but its estimates remain sensitive to architecture and the diffusion-time or noise-scale choice.

competitive_landscape.title: Scale adaptive and robust intrinsic dimension estimation via optimal neighbourhood identification
competitive_landscape.relationship: Adaptive-neighborhood competitor that directly attacks the scale, noise and curvature tradeoff emphasized by the survey.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its ABIDE procedure selects the largest locally constant-density neighborhood without a ground-truth dimension oracle, but it is specialized to constant-dimensional smooth manifolds and nearest-neighbor likelihood assumptions rather than universal method selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic Dimension Estimation Using Wasserstein Distances
competitive_landscape.relationship: Theory-focused estimator with finite-sample nonasymptotic guarantees based on Wasserstein distances between empirical measures.
competitive_landscape.difference: The survey mentions this family but does not benchmark it; it offers guarantees under explicit assumptions rather than the paper's broad empirical ranking, at higher computational and modeling cost.

competitive_landscape.title: Topological Singularity Detection at Multiple Scales
competitive_landscape.relationship: Multi-scale local method that jointly estimates intrinsic dimension and deviation from Euclidean manifold structure.
competitive_landscape.difference: It can flag singular or non-manifold regions rather than presuming one smooth global dimension, directly addressing a benchmark assumption left largely untested in the reviewed paper.

competitive_landscape.title: CW Complex Hypothesis for Image Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing structural hypothesis and empirical study in which local intrinsic dimension varies across points within a connected image-data component.
competitive_landscape.difference: It challenges the constant smooth-manifold target underlying most of the survey benchmark and motivates stratified or cell-complex outputs instead of a single ground-truth d.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust estimation of the intrinsic dimension of data sets with quantum cognition machine learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Spectral-gap estimator emphasizing robustness to noise and evaluations on real datasets.
competitive_landscape.difference: It extends beyond the survey's narrow synthetic noise generators, but has its own Hilbert-space dimension and loss choices and is mentioned only briefly rather than included in the matched cohort.

competitive_landscape.title: On consistent estimation of dimension values
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous theory competitor proving consistency and some rates for Minkowski, correlation and pointwise-dimension estimators.
competitive_landscape.difference: It contributes formal guarantees and an empirical study where the reviewed paper primarily synthesizes prior theory and supplies a wider implementation benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: A Survey and Comparative Evaluation of Intrinsic Dimension Estimators under the Manifold Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Independent direct successor survey with eighteen manifolds, one hundred replicates, nonuniformity, noise and real ISOMAP, MNIST and ISOLET studies.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its stability-based per-dataset tuning and different estimator panel recommend CA-PCA and TwoNN as defaults with DANCo as a third opinion, demonstrating that recommendations depend strongly on cohort, tuning and benchmark design.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantum-inspired Benchmark for Estimating Intrinsic Dimension
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct successor benchmark using infinite families of topologically nontrivial homogeneous spaces, multiple embeddings, controllable curvature and noise, and a fractal case.
competitive_landscape.difference: Six estimators are generally less accurate on QuIIEst than on standard benchmarks under equal resources, supporting the survey's anti-universality message while showing that its inherited sphere-and-cube-like suite is not sufficiently discriminating.

competitive_landscape.title: Score-based Pullback Riemannian Geometry: Extracting the Data Manifold Geometry using Anisotropic Flows
competitive_landscape.relationship: Geometry-rich score-model alternative that estimates tangent geometry, metric, charts, geodesics and intrinsic dimension jointly.
competitive_landscape.difference: It moves beyond scalar dimension estimation toward recovering manifold geometry from learned anisotropic flows, at the cost of model training and score-quality assumptions absent from classical estimators.

competitive_landscape.title: Mutual Information and Task-Relevant Latent Dimensionality
competitive_landscape.relationship: Successor that changes the estimand from geometric support dimension to the number of latent directions informative for a downstream task.
competitive_landscape.difference: It addresses cases where noise or nuisance variation makes classical support dimension unhelpful; it is not a drop-in replacement because task-relevant dimension answers a different question.

competitive_landscape.title: Local Hessian Spectral Filtering for Robust Intrinsic Dimension Estimation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later score-and-Hessian method designed for robust high-codimension local dimension estimation with stochastic spectral computation.
competitive_landscape.difference: It targets aggregate-signal failures of LIDL and FLIPD and reports improved synthetic and real robustness, so the survey's nonlinear-above-six finding should remain explicitly limited to its tested methods rather than projected onto later approaches.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents the first broad survey of intrinsic-dimension estimation in roughly nine years, introduces a geometric-information taxonomy, expands scikit-dimension with additional classical and topological estimators, and supplies a wide practical study of sample size, hyperparameters, noise, curvature and estimator failure.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The 72-page article develops three estimator families, documents added implementations, evaluates a large method-by-manifold-by-setting grid, isolates neighborhood throttling, and includes full per-dataset and hyperparameter appendices. However, 2015-2016 surveys already supplied method taxonomies, ideal-estimator criteria and synthetic benchmark frameworks, and the 2021 scikit-dimension paper already supplied a unified tested package and a benchmark exceeding 500 datasets. Pre-submission CA-PCA, adaptive-neighborhood, consistency and modern learned methods also delimit coverage, while later independent surveys and topology-rich benchmarks produce different rankings.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the integration of a geometric-information taxonomy with post-2015 and topological coverage, a substantially expanded common implementation, and unusually detailed controlled analysis of tuning, throttling, sample size, noise and curvature. It is not the first taxonomy, benchmark, survey or unified package. Its ESS and nonlinear-dimension conclusions are valuable cohort-specific observations, not universal rankings; formula errors, in-sample oracle selection, narrow topology and incomplete experiment release materially limit stronger claims.

reviewer_notes: Primary review read all 72 pages of the exact archived PDF, including pages 1-38 of main text, all 116 bibliography entries on pages 39-45, appendices on pages 46-72, every formula-bearing page, all 24 numbered figures, and all table-bearing pages. Every page was rendered at 110 dpi and visually audited; the landscape tables on pages 52-65 were additionally rotated upright for inspection, and the hyperparameter and noise matrices on pages 66-72 were checked visually against their captions. The audit recomputed the disputed lPCA, capacity, TwoNN and ball-sphere Wasserstein relations, checked the Appendix C selection definition, and distinguished author results from reviewer inference. Current primary-source competitor research was checked through 2026-08-23 and includes direct predecessors, omitted pre-cutoff methods, an independent successor survey, topology-rich stress benchmarks, score-based estimators and a distinct task-relevant estimand. The linked https://github.com/kmyim/scikit-dimension default branch was inspected at commit d7c6248a591b761373dbeb3abbcb32ed2c83c232 on 2026-08-23; it contains reusable library code, documentation, tests and CI but not a pinned, complete reproduction bundle for the paper's reported experiments.
